<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="DjR" /></noinclude><section begin="par112"/>'' maiden which cometh forth'' ({{GHGheb|text=הַיֹּצֵאת}})... {{GHGheb|text=וְאָֽמַרְתִּי אֵלֶ֫יהָ|translate=to whom I shall say}}..., {{GHGheb|text=וְאָֽמְרָה|translate=and she}} (then) ''shall say'', &c. This use of the perfect consecutive is especially frequent after a participle introduced by {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=6|verse=17}} f.; with a different subject {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=20|verse=36}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=6|verse=14}}; after a complete noun-clause introduced by {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה}} (cf. § 140), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=3|verse=13}} ''behold, I come'' (i.e. if I shall come)... {{GHGheb|text=וְאָֽמַרְתִּי לָהֶם|translate=and shall say unto them}}..., {{GHGheb|text=וְאָֽמְרוּ|translate=and they}} (then) ''shall say'', &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=14|verse=8}} ff., {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=7|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=8|verse=7|hidebook=1}} f., 39:6.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|u}}
(ζ) After an infinitive absolute, whether the infinitive absolute serves to strengthen the finite verb (see {{GHGpar|113|t}}), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=31|verse=5}}, or is used as an emphatic substitute for a cohortative or imperfect ({{GHGpar|113|dd}} and ''ee''), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=2|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=1|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=23|verse=46}} f.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|v}}
(η) After an infinitive construct governed by a preposition (for this change from the infinitive construction to the finite verb, cf. {{GHGpar|114|r}}), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=10|verse=8}} {{GHGheb|text=עַד־בּוֹאִי אֵלֶ֫יךָ וְהֽוֹדַעְתִּי לְךָ|translate=till I come unto thee}} (prop. until my coming) ''and show thee'', &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=45|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=6|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=39|verse=27}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=2|verse=37}}, 42.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|w}}
Rem. To the same class belong {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=14|verse=24}}, where the idea of time precedes, ''until it be evening and'' until ''I be avenged'', &c., and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=5|verse=8}}, where the idea of place precedes, in both cases governed by {{GHGheb|text=עַד־}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|112|x}}
'''4.''' The very frequent use of the perfect consecutive in direct dependence upon other tenses (see above, ''d''–''v'') explains how it finally obtained a kind of independent force—especially for the purpose of announcing future events—and might depend loosely on sentences to which it stood only in a wider sense in the relation of a temporal or logical consequence. Thus the perfect consecutive is used—

(''a'') To announce ''future'' events, &c., in loose connexion with a further announcement, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=41|verse=30}} {{GHGheb|text=וְקָמוּ}} and two co-ordinate perfects consecutive, equivalent to ''but then shall arise'', &c.; frequently so after {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה}} with a following substantive ({{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=9|verse=8}}), or a participial clause (cf. the analogous instances above, under ''t''), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=31}} ''behold, the days come'', {{GHGheb|text=וְגָֽדַעְתִּי|translate=that I will cut off}}, &c.; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=39|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=4|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=8|verse=11|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=9|verse=13|hidebook=1}}, and very often in Jeremiah; after an expression of time, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=17|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=10|verse=25}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=29|verse=17|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=51|verse=33}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=1|verse=4}}. Further, when joined to a statement concerning present or past facts, especially when these contain the reason for the action, &c., expressed in the perfect consecutive; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=6|verse=7}} ''lo, this hath touched thy lips'', {{GHGheb|text=וְסָר|translate=therefore thine iniquity shall be taken away}}, &c. (not copulative ''and it is taken away'', since it is parallel with a simple imperfect), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=20|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=26|verse=22|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=13|verse=3}} (here in an adversative sense); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=8|verse=14}}. In loose connexion with a noun-clause, a long succession of perfects consecutive occurs in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=6|verse=6}} ff. Also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Amos|chapter=5|verse=26}} {{GHGheb|text=וּנְשָׁאתֶם}} may be an announcement ''yea, ye shall take up''; but cf. below, ''rr''.<section end="par112"/><noinclude>
